Atomic Habits - A Five-Minute Masterclass

This book is not really about habits. It is about identity, about becoming the kind of person who gets the results you want, one tiny decision at a time.

1. Tiny changes compound. Getting 1 percent better every day does not feel like much in the moment, but over a year those small gains multiply into something dramatically different. Habits are the compound interest of self improvement.

2. Systems beat goals. Winners and losers often have the exact same goals, so the goal cannot be what separates them. What matters is the daily system you follow. Fix your inputs and the outputs take care of themselves.

3. Identity change drives lasting change. The most effective way to build a habit is not to focus on what you want to achieve, but on who you wish to become. Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you believe you are.

4. The plateau of latent potential explains why habits seem to fail at first. Progress is often invisible for a long stretch before it suddenly breaks through, like ice cracking after being heated for hours. Do not quit right before the payoff.

5. The four laws of behavior change give you a simple recipe for any habit. Make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy, and make it satisfying. Break any one of those four and the habit falls apart.

6. Make it obvious means designing clear cues. Use implementation intentions, deciding in advance exactly when and where you will act, such as saying I will exercise at 7 a.m. in the living room, rather than leaving it to vague willpower.

7. Habit stacking links a new behavior to one you already do automatically. After I pour my morning coffee, I will meditate for one minute. Your existing routines become the trigger for the new one, so you do not have to rely on memory or motivation.

8. Make it attractive by pairing habits you need with ones you want, and by surrounding yourself with people for whom the desired behavior is normal. We naturally imitate the habits of the close, the many, and the powerful around us.

9. Make it easy is about reducing friction. The number one driver of behavior is not intensity, it is convenience. Shrink a habit down to something that takes two minutes or less to start, because a habit must be established before it can be improved.

10. The two minute rule says any new habit should be scaled down until it can be done in two minutes or less. Read one page, put on your running shoes, write one sentence. Master the art of showing up before you worry about doing it perfectly.

11. Make it satisfying because the brain prioritizes immediate rewards over delayed ones. Add a small, instant reward right after a good habit, and track your progress visually, since nothing feels better than seeing a streak of checkmarks you do not want to break.

12. Environment design shapes behavior more than motivation does. Make good choices visible and convenient, like leaving fruit on the counter, and make bad choices invisible and inconvenient, like unplugging the television or deleting an app. You do not need more willpower, you need a better room.

13. Habits are shaped by the crowd around you, so choose your environment and your circle deliberately. Join groups where your desired behavior is the normal behavior, and the culture will pull you toward it without any extra effort.

14. Never miss twice. Perfection is not the goal, recovery speed is. If you slip once, that is an accident, but if you let it happen twice, it starts becoming a new pattern. Get back on track immediately and the occasional miss will not matter in the long run.

In the end, you do not rise to the level of your goals, you fall to the level of your systems. Small habits do not add up, they compound. Decide who you want to become, then let your daily actions cast the votes. Change the system, and the results change themselves.
